mainClaim: Remote work increases productivity for most knowledge workers while improving work-life balance
evidence: Bloom, Liang, Roberts and Ying (Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2015) ran a nine-month experiment at Ctrip, a 16,000-employee Chinese travel agency. Call center employees who volunteered to work from home were randomly assigned to work from home or in the office. Home working led to a 13% performance increase, of which 9% came from working more minutes per shift (fewer breaks and sick days) and 4% from more calls per minute. Home workers also reported better work satisfaction and their attrition rate halved, but their promotion rate conditional on performance fell.
supportingPoints: Reduced office distractions allow for longer periods of deep focus work
Flexibility enables work during peak cognitive hours (varies by individual)
Geographic flexibility allows hiring best talent regardless of location
Environmental benefits: 54M tons CO2 reduction from eliminated commutes

sourceMetadata.title: Does Working from Home Work? Evidence from a Chinese Experiment
sourceMetadata.methodology: Randomized experiment among volunteering call center employees at one firm

limitations: The cited experiment covers call center employees at one Chinese firm who volunteered. It does not establish that remote work raises productivity for most knowledge workers. Results vary significantly by role type - creative collaboration may suffer. Junior employees benefit less without in-person mentorship. Requires discipline and proper home workspace. Hybrid models may capture best of both approaches.
